title: Input and Output
description: Reading user input and formatting output using print(), f-strings, and format().
objectives: Format output using f-strings and str.format()
Control print() behavior with sep and end
Understand escape sequences and the concepts of stdout/stderr

content.heading: print() and input()
content.body:
print() writes its arguments to standard output (stdout), separated by a space by default and ending with a newline. Both behaviors are configurable: print(a, b, sep=", ", end="!\n") changes the separator and the ending. Errors and diagnostic messages conventionally go to standard error (stderr) instead of stdout, via sys.stderr.write(...) or print(..., file=sys.stderr) — this lets a program's real output be separated from its error/log messages when piped or redirected.

input(prompt) displays the optional prompt string, waits for the user to type a line and press Enter, and always returns that line as a str — with no automatic type conversion. Converting to int(), float(), etc. is the caller's responsibility.

content.heading: String Formatting
content.body: Modern Python code almost always uses f-strings (formatted string literals, introduced in Python 3.6): f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}" evaluates the expressions inside {} and inserts their string representation directly. f-strings also support format specifiers, like f"{price:.2f}" for two decimal places. The older str.format() method achieves the same thing with "{} {}".format(a, b), and the oldest %-style formatting ("%d" % 5) still appears in legacy code. Common escape sequences inside string literals include \n (newline), \t (tab), \\ (a literal backslash), and \" (a literal quote inside a double-quoted string).

content.code:
name = "Asha"
score = 92.456
print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f}%")   # Asha scored 92.5%
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-", end="!\n")  # a-b-c!

# input() always returns a string:
# age = int(input("Age: "))
content.explanation: The :.1f format specifier rounds score to one decimal place when inserted into the f-string. sep and end change print()'s default single-space separator and trailing newline.

keyPoints: print() writes to stdout by default; sep and end are configurable
input() always returns a str — convert it explicitly if you need a number
f-strings (f"...{expr}...") are the preferred modern formatting style
Format specifiers like :.2f control numeric display inside f-strings
stderr is conventionally used for errors/diagnostics, separate from normal output
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert input() results before doing arithmetic on them
Mixing up f-string syntax f"{x}" with plain string "{x}" (missing the f prefix)
Assuming print() flushes output immediately in every environment (it usually does for a terminal, but buffering can differ when piped)
